figures.caption: Figure 1: CoupleFlow. The two small signal plots show the input of one real MAESTRO test window (listener S03): seven of its EEG channels and the envelopes of its K = 4 candidate talkers, with the attended talker in dark orange. The neural path (blue) maps the EEG x to an embedding e whose value at time t sees only EEG from t+ δ to t+ δ+0.98 s after the sound (δ ∈ {0, 125}ms). The acoustic path (orange) embeds each candidate k with one shared encoder. The paths meet only in the coupling score sk (Eq. 1), which makes the decision. The flow head (pink) supplies the alternative pointwise-mutual-information (PMI) rule (Prop. 2) and per-source residuals. Tags mark where each loss in Eq. 2 acts, coloured by role: decoding (green), density (pink), anti-shortcut (gold), auxiliary (grey). Dashed: reversed gradient of the audio-only adversary.

Table 1: Accuracy (%) of CoupleFlow (Ours) and the baselines at 1, 5 and 20 s on the content-disjoint folds (every model trained and tested on the same folds), and on unseen listeners (LOSO: listener and content held out, 5 s) against the pooled linear backward model. comp.: attended vs. competing talker; mm: match–mismatch. Ours: mean of 3 seeds (s.d. 0.0–1.8 at 5 s); LOSO: one seed. Bold: best per group. CoupleFlow’s EEG-shuffle nulls lie in [49.7, 50.5] up to 10 s. All windows and per-trial accuracy: App. Table 13; full LOSO results: App. Table 21.
Figure 2: Accuracy vs. window length (log scale). Markers: CoupleFlow (seed 0), pooled over folds. Lines: Φ(κ √ T ) with one κ per curve (Prop. 3).

Table 5: Recent side classifiers, accuracy (%) under their within-trial split / our content-disjoint folds (subject-dependent, as in the papers), next to CoupleFlow on the content-disjoint folds (seed 0). †Ill-posed under content-disjoint folds (one class per listener in each test fold).
Table 6: Failure modes in AAD evaluation, what they inflate, and the control in this work.

Table 7: Datasets after unified preprocessing. Groups: content groups recovered from the audio; folds = min(5, groups). Env.: gammatone envelope computed from the audio (ours) or published by the dataset authors (prov.). HI: hearing-impaired. 1-/2-talker: single talker or two competing talkers.

Table 8: Releases, versions and licenses (checked on the release pages, September 2026). CC: Creative Commons; BY: attribution; NC: non-commercial; SA: share-alike; CC0: public-domain dedication. BIDS: Brain Imaging Data Structure; RDR: Research Data Repository; OSF: Open Science Framework. Excluded datasets are listed for completeness.

Table 9: Content groups recovered from the audio. Groups per listener: how many groups one listener heard. Single-trial groups: content heard in one trial only. Links: 64-Hz-confirmed links that merged two components (trials − groups). Last two columns: best 8-Hz match of a 10-s chunk in another group, and the 64-Hz correlation at that location: the chance level the 0.95 threshold must exceed.
Table 10: Canonical 64 vs. all native channels (5-s and trial accuracy, %; 125-ms lag window, seed 0).

Figure 5: Input, listener correction and virtual sensors. The correction reads two spatial patterns of the EEG with Vm and writes them back with Um; the identity path keeps the shared model, and Um = 0 at initialisation, so a listener departs from it only as far as the data require. Bottom: maps from the KU Leuven fold-0 checkpoint, namely Vm and Um of the listener with the largest correction, and the activation patterns ΣW⊤(WΣW⊤)−1 of the eight virtual sensors, with W their weights and Σ the covariance of the corrected training EEG (Haufe et al., 2014). Diverging colour scale per map, grey at zero.

Table 11: CoupleFlow modules and parameter counts (KU Leuven checkpoint; ∗envelope-only input). GN: GroupNorm; GELU: Gaussian error linear unit; MLP: multilayer perceptron. Only the rows in the decision path are needed at test time for the coupling decision; the flow head is needed for the PMI rule.

Figure 6: Receptive fields of both encoders on one time axis, drawn to scale (one dot per sample at 64Hz; each node depends on three nodes of the layer below, spaced by the dilation d). The neural embedding et reads EEG from δ to δ + 0.98 s after the sound at t (blue; δ = 125ms shown, 0ms on six datasets, chosen on validation), and the candidate embedding âk,t reads the 0.48 s of audio up to t (orange). Matching the two therefore fixes the lag direction: the brain response must follow the sound. The lag control uses the mirrored window before the sound (hatched). Each decision window carries 100 samples (1.56 s) of context on both sides, more than either receptive field needs, so no output depends on zero padding.

Figure 9: Flow head. (a) Training: the velocity network sees the noisy envelope a(u) on the straight path from noise ε to the attended envelope a, the neural embedding (dropped with probability 0.2), a flag saying whether it is present, and the flow time u, and regresses the path velocity a− ε. (b) Test: every candidate is scored with and without the neural embedding on the same Monte-Carlo draws; the difference of the residuals estimates its pointwise mutual information with the recording (Prop. 2).

Figure 10: Auxiliary heads. (a) The side head reads only the listener-corrected EEG; its side log-probabilities enter the training loss through the candidate scores but never the reported accuracies, which use the coupling score alone. (b) The audio-only adversary tries to find the attended candidate from the audio embeddings; the gradient-reversal layer (GRL) passes its gradient to the audio encoder with the sign flipped, so the encoder removes any such cue. (c) The envelope read-out reports reconstruction accuracy and is not used by any decision rule.

Table 12: Weighted loss terms during training (each already multiplied by its weight; mean over folds and seeds of the logged epoch average), at the first epoch and at the selected epoch. Chance: value of a term for a decoder at chance (K = 2 candidates, batch B = 32). “–”: the side head needs two talkers in known positions. Five Broderick runs evaluated from saved checkpoints have no logged history and are omitted.

Table 13: CoupleFlow and every baseline at every window (%, content-disjoint folds, pooled over all test windows; competing talker for two-talker sets, match–mismatch for SparrKULee and MEG-MASC). CoupleFlow: mean of 3 seeds with the validation-chosen lag window, as in Table 1; “CoupleFlow, mm”: match–mismatch on the two-talker recordings. trial: one decision per trial. “–”: window longer than the trials. CoupleFlow nulls: 49.7–50.5% up to 10 s; 42.5–61.1% at 20–60 s, where few windows exist. DECAF, trained with the same folds and selection rule, stays near chance on the two-talker sets.
Table 14: Change in 5-s accuracy (points) when one component is removed; full model: mean±s.d. over 3 seeds, 125-ms lag window; variants: seed 0.

Table 15: Content leakage: 5-s competing accuracy (%) when folds share stories (trial split: whole trials held out, but the stories of test trials also occur in training trials) against content-disjoint folds. Every model is retrained on each split. CoupleFlow: seed 0, 125-ms lag window on both splits.

Table 16: Recent side classifiers (authors’ models in our training pipeline), accuracy (%) under their within-trial split (last 10% of each trial held out for testing; earlier windows split 9:1 into training and validation) and under our content-disjoint folds, subject-dependent and subject-independent. On KU Leuven the content-disjoint side task is ill-posed (one class per listener in each test fold).

Table 18: Ablation on MAESTRO, where the audio offers a shortcut (the attended talker is always the loudest): within listeners, seed 0, 4-way. For each variant: 5-s accuracy and contribution with unmatched candidates (shortcut available) and with matched candidates; the EEG-shuffle and circular-shift nulls; per-trial accuracy and contribution; and embedding collapse (mean cosine between windows; 1 = every window alike).

Table 19: CoupleFlow variants, 5-s accuracy (%, seed 0). 125ms / 0ms: start of the neural lag window. env. only: broadband envelope without sub-band features (Fuglsang’20 and Broderick are envelope-only in every column). rank 8: larger per-listener correction. listener FT: per-listener fine-tuning after pooled training. native ch.: all native channels instead of the 64 canonical ones (125-ms window). n/a: the variant equals the base (envelope-only releases; caps with 64 EEG channels). “–”: not run. Rank 8 and listener FT were run only on KU Leuven, DTU and ESAA, to test whether listener heterogeneity explained the ESAA gap; neither did. MEG-MASC uses its 208 sensors throughout (208-channel input layer).

Table 20: Test of Prop. 3: tracking of the attended (ratt) and competing (rcomp) envelope by the per-listener linear decoder (all listeners), ignored-talker ratio γ, the predicted and the observed ratio of competing to match– mismatch κ.

Table 21: Leave-one-listener-out (LOSO) accuracy (%), listener and content held out together, one seed. Content folds: the main-table 5-s accuracy (3 seeds) for reference. Null: EEG from another trial of the same listener (another window of the same trial when the listener has a single test trial). Linear: pooled ridge backward model on the same folds (two-talker sets; penalty chosen on the first 40 validation segments). a208-sensor input (App. D). MAESTRO’s LOSO results are in Sec. 4.

Figure 11: Accuracy against mean decision time, two-talker datasets (test folds). Fixed: sign of the summed calibrated log-odds of T consecutive 1-s windows. Sequential: the rule of Prop. 8 at thresholds A = 0.25, . . . , 5. Dotted: Wald’s prediction from CoupleFlow’s fitted κ (Prop. 8). CoupleFlow: mean of 3 seeds.

Table 22: Calibration and combination of windows (test folds; mean of 3 seeds unless marked). ECE: expected calibration error, 10 bins; NLL: log-loss in bits (chance 1). ens.: average of the 3 seeds’ calibrated log-odds. Trial: one decision per trial by majority vote of the 5-s windows or by the sign of their summed log-odds. Last two columns: diagnostics of Prop. 6 on the 1-s log-odds.

Figure 12: Effect of the threshold A. (a) Accuracy of the decisions that reached the threshold, against the guarantee Λ(A) (dashed). (b) Mean chosen length. (c) Share of decisions cut by the end of a trial.

Table 24: Anatomy of the sequential rule (CoupleFlow, calibrated 1-s log-odds, 3 seeds pooled, test folds). Λ(A): accuracy guaranteed by Prop. 9 for decisions that reach the threshold. Accuracy of all decisions and of those that reached the threshold (decided). Chosen length: mean, median and 10th–90th percentile of the number of seconds a decision used. Forced: share and accuracy of decisions cut by the end of a trial. Fixed: fixed-length accuracy at the same mean length; gain in points.

Figure 13: The chosen decision length. (a) Share of decisions taken within a given number of seconds, for four thresholds; markers: medians. (b) Accuracy of the decisions that reached the threshold, grouped by the length they used, for A = 1, 2, 3. Dotted: Λ(A), the accuracy Prop. 9 guarantees for every length. Bins with fewer than 20 decisions are omitted.

Figure 14: Overlapping 1-s windows (CoupleFlow, seed 0, test folds): the sequential rule on h/w-scaled log-odds with hop h = 1, 0.5 and 0.25 s, restarting after each decision at the first window disjoint from it, and fixed-length decisions (nearly identical for every hop; the hop-1 s curve is shown).

Figure 15: Test accuracy against test window for CoupleFlow trained on 1-, 2-, 5- (paper), 10-s crops or a length redrawn from {1, 2, 5, 10} s every epoch; everything else as in the paper (selection on 5-s validation windows). Mean of 3 seeds, test folds; competing talker for two-talker sets, match–mismatch for SparrKULee and MEG-MASC.
Table 26: Training-window ablation: accuracy (%, mean±s.d. over 3 seeds) at 1-, 5- and 30-s test windows, κ of the summed 1-s log-odds, and the sequential rule at A=2 (two-talker sets).
